John Alden was not one of the Pilgrims.
Governor Bradford’s list of the passengers says he “was hired for a cooper, at Southampton,
where the ship victualled; and being a hopeful young man, was much desired, but left to his own liking to go or stay
when he came here; but he stayed, and married here.”
A cooper kept the barrels sound, and the beer and water with them.
He signed the Mayflower Compact in Provincetown harbor, married Priscilla Mullins,
and moved across the bay to Duxbury, where for most of fifty years he sat as one of the governor’s assistants and
for a time kept the colony’s treasury. In 1634 a quarrel over the fur trade on the Kennebec River left two men shot
dead. Alden had been there on the colony’s bark, though Bradford says he “was no actor in the business”,
and when he put in at Boston the Massachusetts men locked him up.
Plymouth sent Captain Standish with letters, and Thomas Dudley set him free.
He died at Duxbury on 12 September 1687, by the usual count the last of the men who had signed the Compact.
Five years later his son, Captain John Alden of Boston, was accused of witchcraft at Salem;
he broke out of jail, hid, and was cleared the next year.
